title: Head arrangements, stock arrangements and who read in Floyd's band
summary: The band used many head arrangements and stocks; only a few could read, and Albert transposed parts from violin, clarinet or piano.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well, how did he play then? Did he use many head arrangements? Would he just be faking all the time or what? I don't know.

A lot of head arrangements and the piano player was a good reading musician, not a hell of a piano player, but a good reading musician. Then he had, well, Ben O'Kennedy, who was the trumpet player, was a seasoned musician. He was great. And I imagined through him and the piano player and the drummer who could read and Charlie Dixon, who could read. And Troy was a good reader. Troy could read, but he wasn't much of a player, but a good reader. And that way they got together and they rehearsed the numbers and I guess just naturally they knew what they were doing.

In listening to their recordings, you know, of the Shadowland and Dreamland blues, I had to hear things, it sounds like they're doing a lot of playing by ear. They are. On those particular recordings.

There weren't any written arrangements as far as that's concerned, unless it was what we call stock arrangements. And everybody didn't read? No. In fact when they were playing, when we had to play the big shows with Troy S. Ben, I had to use the piano part, the violin part, the trumpet part, and the clarinet part. And Pete jumped from one to the other to fit in to make the music right for the performance we were playing for. Could you transpose it? Sure, I can transpose it aside. I can transpose it from a violin part, from a clarinet part, or from a piano part. Also from an alto part.
